newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: SE Asian Grains - Buyers back-off on Chicago rally.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grains - Buyers back-off on Chicago rally.

text.p: The surge in U.S. soybean futures to 8-1/2 year highs and the corresponding rally in Chicago corn prices has kept most regional buyers sidelined ahead of USDA stocks data due later on Tuesday, traders said.
"Buyers are still well covered at the moment," a trader at a major Malaysian flour mill said.
He said the market has ample stocks of corn and other grains and meal following heavy buying before the Chinese Lunar New Year and Moslem Eid al-Fitr festivals in February.
"Some are covered up to May. But there are also some who are only starting to cover their positions. They have no choice but to buy as prices may go higher," another trader said.

Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) soybean and soymeal futures soared to 8-1/2 year highs on Monday on expectations that the USDA will cut its 1996/97 ending stocks estimate later on Tuesday exacerbating an already tight supply situation.
CBOT corn futures rallied to a 5-1/2 month peak on Monday, dragged higher by the surge in the soy complex.
Malaysian traders said they expect the USDA to release smaller 1996/97 soybean ending stocks figures maintaining the upward momentum in world prices.
"I think it will still be bullish. Crops from Argentina will only reach the market in May and until then prices should remain firm," one said.
He said some Indian origin soymeal is likely in Malaysia soon but "this should be easily absorbed by the market."
In Thailand, oil crushers and feed millers seeking April and May cargoes of soybeans and soymeal were sidelined in the past week by the surge in Chicago prices, local trade sources said.
But despite high prices, one oil crusher was said to have bought 50,000 tonnes of optional-origin soybeans late last week for March/April shipment to cover near-term demand.
Otherwise the market bought hand-to-mouth with the focus on soymeal substitutes such as sunflower and groundnut meals, trade sources said.
"The US prices are high, the Brazil prices are high and the freight is also high. What am I in this market for? There is no buyer," said one Bangkok-based trader.

Despite high demand, however, the industry can afford to stay away from the market, at least for now, as between 160,000-200,000 tonnes of domestic soybeans are expected to enter the domestic market soon.
"That (local soybean supply) would probably last until May. The industry will have to cover their June-July demand soon," said another trader.

"My trading philosophy is people have to eat. Even though the prices are high, the industry will have to book April/May shipment soon. They might be able to sideline for now, but we expect them in the market in a very near future," he said.

In Indonesia, domestic corn prices rose on Tuesday in a knee-jerk response to the overnight rally in Chicago, which could keep local buyers sidelined momentarily, but offers from China were seen as tempting.
Traders said Chinese suppliers were offering April Handy-sized shipments at around $150-$152 a tonne C&F.
"I have been offered between 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes of Chinese corn at $150-$152 per tonne for April shipments," one trader said. "I think it is a good price, at the moment."

"But I think most feedmills will be staying out of the market for the moment following the gains in Chicago yesterday," he said. "Many feedmills have missed the boat, having not booked corn earlier as they thought prices were high."
Another trader said U.S. corn was quoted before the Chicago rally at $153 a tonne C&F for Handy-sized vessels and at $145 for Panamax cargoes.
"I heard some feedmills are looking for May/June corn, but I think orders will not be made anytime now because of the rally in Chicago," the trader said.
Traders said some local corn suppliers had begun to hold back transactions following the U.S. price increases.
They said Indonesian corn was quoted at 400-410 rupiah a kg in Jakarta, against 390 rupiah a week ago.
Traders said soymeal prices were generally stable on steady demand, but added that the market could be heading to an oversupply situation that could weaken prices.
"Feedmills are currently eating out their stocks before having to decide on imports," one trader said. "Plenty of Indian origin soymeal is continuing to arrive in Indonesia."
The trader said Indian soymeal was quoted at $326 C&F.
Data from Tanjung Priok Port showed that the Yong An I was scheduled to arrive at the Jakarta port on March 17 with some 30,000 tonnes of soybeans from the United States.
Data from Belawan Port showed that the MV Bureba arrived at the North Sumatran port on Sunday with 12,000 tonnes of soymeal from India.
